title: Writing a risk assessment for height work
audience: Supervisors, leading hands and workers who write, check or sign off a work-at-height plan for a service job.
learningOutcomes: Identify each height-related hazard in a task, using the positions, routes, equipment and conditions.
Choose and record the control for each hazard using the hierarchy in “The hierarchy of controls for height work”.
Write a work-at-height plan that names the rescue arrangement, the people, and the stop-work conditions.
Recognise an incomplete or unreasoned plan, and return it for correction.

instruction.heading: Planning comes before the climb
instruction.body: A plan for height work is set down before anybody leaves the ground. The sources agree on several points: hazards are identified before work begins, the most suitable equipment is chosen, the weather is taken into account, the people doing the work are competent, the hazards from fragile surfaces and falling objects are managed, and equipment is inspected before and during use. A risk assessment serves as the written record of that planning, and one source requires it to be written before height work starts.

instruction.heading: What the assessment must cover
instruction.body: A height assessment covers the task and its duration, the positions and heights, the access route, the surfaces and their condition, the equipment and its inspection, the people and their training, the weather and its limits, the rescue arrangement, the public and people below, and the stop-work conditions. Record each hazard as one line, with the likelihood and severity scores used in the business's scheme (see “Scoring a hazard: likelihood, severity and the risk band”), the control, and the residual risk (see “Ranking controls and checking residual risk”).

instruction.heading: Scoring a fall
instruction.body: Score a fall by the height, the surface below, and the likely injury. A short fall onto a hard surface can be serious, and a fall onto a clear surface can still injure with a bad landing. Do not lower the score because a control is planned. Score the risk as it stands, and then score the residual risk after the control is in place and has been checked. Write the reason beside each score, so that a reviewer can follow it.

instruction.heading: Choosing the controls in the plan
instruction.body: For each hazard, write the highest feasible control from the hierarchy in “The hierarchy of controls for height work”, and the reason any higher option was rejected. Name each physical control to be inspected, such as the guardrail, platform, scaffold, tower or ladder, and each personal control with its type and its rescue method. Do not list a control that will not be on site on the day.

instruction.heading: Cross-checking the plan against the specific lessons
instruction.body: Check the plan against the lessons that match its equipment: ladders (“Choosing and using ladders for trade and exterior work”), scaffolds and towers (“Scaffold and mobile tower checks before use”), mobile elevated platforms (“Elevated work platform pre-use checks”), roofs and fragile surfaces (“Roof and fragile-surface work”), edges and openings (“Edge protection, floor openings and covers”), and rescue (“Suspension trauma and rescue planning”). Check that every state or territory rule in those lessons has been confirmed before the plan relies on it.

instruction.heading: Briefing and sign-off
instruction.body: The plan is briefed before work starts. Everyone involved should know the plan, their role, the rescue arrangement and the stop-work conditions. The supervisor signs off where the business requires it, and the record goes with the job. The height-work authorisation record (“Height-work authorisation record”) records the day's checks and any negative responses.

instruction.heading: When the plan is not enough
instruction.body: A plan that cannot be carried out safely must be changed or stopped. Examples include equipment that cannot be set up on the surface, a rescue arrangement that is not ready, weather that turns, or a control that is missing. Stop, make the area safe, and tell the supervisor before continuing.

instruction.heading: The licence and authority boundary
instruction.body: Some elevating equipment and scaffolding work need licences or authorisation in some states, and the rules differ by state. A plan that assumes a licence the worker does not hold is not a valid plan. The state rules are set out in “Scaffold and mobile tower checks before use” and “Elevated work platform pre-use checks”, and they are confirmed only where marked. Completing this lesson grants no authority.

procedure: List each step of the task that involves height, and the position at each step.
For each position, list the fall types, routes and falling-object risks.
Score each hazard as it stands, and write the reason beside each score.
For each hazard, choose the highest feasible control, and write why each higher option was rejected.
Name the rescue arrangement, the people and the equipment.
Write the stop-work conditions and the weather limits.
Check the plan against the specific lessons, and against any state rule not yet checked.
Brief the team, sign off, and keep the record with the job.

workedExamples.situation: A small team plans to replace an exterior light fitting under an eave about four metres high. They have two ladders and a platform available.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What would a defensible plan contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: It names the eave height and the access route, and scores the fall and the falling light fitting. It rejects ground-based methods only with a reason, and selects the platform over the ladder for the reach needed. It names the rescue method and the stop conditions, checks the platform against “Elevated work platform pre-use checks”, and leaves the state rule out until it is checked.

workedExamples.situation: A supervisor's plan for a high gutter clean says "use harness" and nothing else.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is missing, and what should happen to the plan?
workedExamples.reasoning: The plan has no hazard list, no reason for skipping higher controls, no rescue arrangement, no equipment inspection and no stop-work conditions. It is returned for correction and does not go ahead in its current form.

equipmentAndPpe: Risk assessment form or register (see “Site risk assessment worksheet” for the site worksheet)

commonErrors.error: Writing a harness as the only control.
commonErrors.prevention: Work down the hierarchy and record each step, including the ones rejected.

commonErrors.error: Writing a rescue plan that does not fit the site.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the access, the equipment and the people for that specific site.

commonErrors.error: Copying a plan from another job without checking the site.
commonErrors.prevention: Reassess each site, because the surface, the weather and the access change.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Warning: height work does not start until the plan is complete, the controls have been set up and checked, and the rescue arrangement is ready.

Licence notice: a risk assessment does not confer a licence or any authority, and a plan that relies on a licence the worker does not hold is not valid. State and territory licence rules are in “Scaffold and mobile tower checks before use” and “Elevated work platform pre-use checks”. Only the positions marked as confirmed there have been checked.

Irish legal references in source 3 are not applicable in Australia and are not used. The UK and Malaysian legal and standards references in sources 2 to 4 are not applicable in Australia and are not used.
NSW: a construction work method statement is required where someone could fall more than two metres (confirmed for NSW, construction work).

qualityStandard: Every height position and route is listed.
Each hazard has a scored entry, with reasons.
Each control is the highest feasible level, with the rejected levels recorded.
The rescue, the people, the equipment and the stop conditions are named.
documentationEvidence: Completed risk assessment for the height task
Link to the height-work authorisation record
summary: Score each hazard as it stands, and again as residual after a verified control.
Choose the highest feasible control, and write down why the others were rejected.
A plan without a rescue arrangement, named people and stop conditions is incomplete.
A plan does not confer a licence or authority; state rules are checked separately.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which of these describes a defensible work-at-height plan?
options: A verbal agreement that the worker is experienced, and the crew, the client and the site manager all agree to it verbally on the day
A written list of positions and routes, scored hazards, the highest feasible controls with reasons, the rescue arrangement and stop conditions.
A harness and a ladder, with no further detail and no rescue or stop rules are listed for the day or the week at all
A plan that scores the risk lower once the controls are simply planned and the controls are never checked on site afterwards by anyone at all

knowledgeChecks.question: A fall is scored with a guardrail planned for it. When should the residual score be used?
options: Before the guardrail is checked and before anyone has seen it
Only after the control is in place and has been checked on site.
Right away, before the guardrail is ordered, from the plan
Only if the job is long and the crew is still working

knowledgeChecks.question: A plan assumes a licence that the worker does not hold. What is the correct outcome?
options: The plan is valid if the worker is willing and the crew agrees to start and the client signs
The plan is not valid, and the job does not proceed on that basis until the licence position is confirmed.
The plan is valid because a licence is not needed for ladders and the worker has used them before
The worker can proceed with a note in the file and the client and the crew have been told
